Thesis Q5 on Kabbalah, now the most discussed of Pico’s 900 propositions, was utterly unintelligible to his judges in Rome and completely detached from the scholastic philosophizing that informed all the other condemned theses—except one, Q7 on Origen. In the broadest sense, all the theses were disputational in intent, and the pattern of all but Q5 and Q7 is the quaestio form of medieval commentaries, quodlibets and summas. but Q5 and Q7 is the quaestio form of medieval commentaries, quodlibets and summas. The form of Q5 reﬂects its own exotic content, however, while Q7’s format is more like a polemic by Eusebius than a summa by Aquinas, and the content of Q7 is philological. If the whole Apology were like Q7, scholars would now see Pico’s book as foreshadowing the achievements of Erasmus in patristic philology—a humanist undertaking motivated, in part, by historical conscious- ness and realized by historical methods. For one thing, Pico stretches the mode of disputation to its limits in showing that the exercise of the mind, not petriﬁed conclusions, is the aim of such debates. This was also his strategy in the imputed defense of Origen (4>29).
